conceptTag: Should a company take a big loan?
readerTitle: The bank said yes. Can you pay it back in a bad year?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (원예용품 매장 확장 대출, 청소 서비스 회사 차량 구입) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 대출 결정은 좋은 해에 얼마를 더 버느냐가 아니라, 나쁜 해에 매달 갚을 현금이 어디서 나오느냐로 판단한다.
misconception: 새 사업이 이자보다 많이 벌기만 하면 대출은 이득이다. 장부상 이익이 나면 대출 상환은 문제없다.

sources.text: 재무관리의 표준 개념 (레버리지, 유동성, 원리금 균등 상환)

factChecks.note: 대출 상환액: $200,000, 연 8%, 5년(60개월) 원리금 균등 상환 시 월 약 $4,055, 연 약 $48,660. 카드에는 월 약 $4,050, 연 약 $48,600으로 반올림. 첫해 이자는 계산상 약 $14,800이며 카드에는 약 $15,000으로 표기.
현금 부족 계산: 첫해 원금 상환 $48,600 − $15,000 = $33,600(약 $34,000). 나쁜 해 이자 후 이익 $20,000 − 원금 $33,600 = 약 −$13,600(약 $14,000 부족). 세금, 감가상각, 재고 변화는 단순화를 위해 제외했습니다.
금리 8% → 6% 인하 시 첫해 이자 절감은 대략 $3,700 수준. 카드에는 'a few thousand dollars'로만 표기.

cards.title: The bank said yes. Can you pay it back in a bad year?
body: Mara runs a busy garden centre. She has put $200,000 of her own money into it, and in a normal year it earns about $40,000.
Her bank offers $200,000 at 8%, repaid over five years, to open a second store. The approval took one day. The hard part is deciding whether to sign.

image.label: Garden centre owner holding a loan letter at the counter
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 화분과 묘목이 가득한 원예용품 매장 계산대에서 주인이 은행 승인 편지를 들고 고민하는 모습. 창밖으로 비어 있는 두 번째 점포가 보임. 실제 은행·브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which question should Mara answer first?
body: The loan costs about $4,050 a month. Mara has one evening to think before she meets the bank.

options.text: Can I get the rate down from 8% to 6%?
options.feedback: Worth asking, and it saves a few thousand dollars a year. But the rate rarely decides whether a loan sinks a business. The fixed monthly payment does.

options.text: If the new store has a bad year, where does each monthly payment come from?
options.feedback: This tests the two things that matter: how **leverage** hurts in a bad year, and whether the cash to pay is actually within reach.

options.text: How much more stock can $200,000 buy?
options.feedback: It plans the spending and skips the repaying. More stock is the reason to borrow, not proof you can pay it back.

cards.title: Debt makes good years better and bad years worse.
body: Return on Mara's own $200,000. In a good year each store earns $40,000. In a bad year the old store earns $25,000 and the new one $10,000. First-year interest is about $15,000 either way.
cards.callout: The interest doesn't shrink when sales do.

cards.title: Borrowed money stretches the result in both directions.
body: **Leverage** means using borrowed money to grow. The lender gets a fixed payment. Mara keeps whatever is left, good or bad.

In a good year, the new store's profit flows to her and her return jumps from 20% to 32.5%. In a bad year, the interest still has to be paid, so her return falls below what she'd have earned without the loan.
cards.softwareNote: A subscription business with steady monthly revenue can carry debt more safely than one that lives on a few large deals. The test is the same: can the payments be made in the worst month, not the average one?

cards.title: Profitable on paper, short of cash in the bank.
body: The $200,000 goes into shelves, fittings and plants. None of it turns back into cash quickly. But the bank wants cash every month, including the principal, the borrowed amount itself. In a bad year, that leaves a hole.

breakdown.label: Principal
breakdown.detail: Paid from cash, not shown as a cost

cards.callout: Assets you can't sell fast don't pay monthly bills.
cards.softwareNote: Money spent building a product works the same way: it's hard to turn back into cash, while loan payments arrive every month.

cards.title: Saying no to debt has a cost too.
body: Refusing every loan protects the bad year but gives up the good one. Over several decent years, Mara's extra return could be large.
The point isn't to avoid debt. It's to size and shape it so a bad year hurts but doesn't break the business. Debt fits best when earnings are steady and some cash stays easy to reach.
These numbers also skip tax and the bank's terms. And a bad year is not the worst year.

cards.title: Now it's a cleaning company.
body: Your office-cleaning firm wins a two-year contract with a business park. You need four vans and equipment: $120,000. The client can cancel with 60 days' notice.

options.text: Borrow $120,000 over five years and buy everything outright
options.feedback: **Leverage** boosts your return while the contract runs. But payments last three years longer than the work is promised, and used vans sell at a loss when you need cash fast.

options.text: Borrow less, rent some vans, and keep three months of payments in cash
options.feedback: You keep most of the upside and limit the downside. The cash reserve is **liquid**, so a cancelled contract gives you time instead of a crisis.

options.text: Turn the contract down to stay debt-free
options.feedback: No repayment risk at all. But you give up two years of profit that a smaller, well-shaped loan could have captured.

cards.title: Judge a loan by the bad year, not the good one.
body: Concepts used: **Leverage**, which stretches results both ways, and **liquid vs illiquid assets**, which decides whether you can pay when sales dip.
**Try it today:** take any loan you have or are considering. Write down a bad year's profit, then the full yearly payment. Where would the difference come from?
